title: Sikh painting
hook: from miniature painters to modern artists like Sobha Singh

segments.voice: Yesterday, gurmat sangeet, the schools that teach the ragas, and Malar, the cooling one. Your line was keeping the ragas. What small skill did you keep alive? Day one thousand three hundred forty-eight.

A framed picture on the wall of a Punjabi living room. An old man with a white beard, eyes half closed, one hand raised in blessing, light gathering around his head. Grandparents walk past it every morning, and it's easy to grow up taking it as a likeness. But that face came from an artist's devotion and imagination. Behind that picture is a long line of painters who tried to put faith into color, from tiny miniatures to large modern canvases. Today's word is their work.
screen: `A PICTURE ON THE LIVING-ROOM WALL.` → `NOBODY PAINTED HIM FROM LIFE.` → `A LONG LINE OF PAINTERS.`

segments.voice: First, the small pictures. Illustrated janamsakhis, the life stories of Guru Nanak, show him in little scenes: under a tree, on a road with Mardana and his rabab, talking with holy men. Later, painters trained in the miniature styles of the Punjab hills worked for Sikh courts, painting rulers, Gurus and stories in fine detail with tiny brushes. Second, the modern canvas. In more recent times, painters like Sobha Singh made large, soft-lit portraits of the Gurus. His Guru Nanak, gentle and luminous, is the kind of picture that ends up framed in homes and gurdwara halls. Other modern artists paint the panth's history, its martyrs, and Punjab's daily life, each in their own style. Third, an honest question. Since these faces come from devotion and imagination, each one is an artist's offering. Some Sikhs treasure these pictures as a way into devotion. Others are cautious, and ask that a painting never be bowed to or treated as the Guru, because for Sikhs the Guru today is the Guru Granth Sahib and the Word. Both are said with care. Fourth, what no paint can hold. The Mool Mantar, the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib, speaks of God as akaal moorat: in paraphrase, a form beyond time. A painting can show a Guru as an artist imagines him. It can't show the one the Guru pointed to. And maybe that's the gift these pictures can give: they point past themselves. Faith in paint, held lightly.
screen: `JANAMSAKHIS AND HILL MINIATURES.` · `SOBHA SINGH'S GURU NANAK.` · `NO ONE PAINTED THEM FROM LIFE.` · `AKAAL MOORAT: BEYOND TIME.` · then, large: `FAITH IN PAINT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a Sikh painting closely. Settle, and breathe. If you can, find one: a janamsakhi scene, a hill miniature, or a modern portrait. If you can't, bring to mind any painting you've seen of someone holy to anyone. Let your eyes move slowly. The hands. The background. Where the light falls. What did the painter choose to show, and what did they leave out? Then let the picture point you past itself, toward whatever it was trying to honor. The bell holds the time.
Sikh painting. From janamsakhi scenes and hill miniatures to modern portraits like Sobha Singh's: faith offered in color, from devotion and imagination. Today's word.
Your line: faith in paint. Today, look closely at one picture on a wall you pass every day, and ask what its maker was trying to honor. Day one thousand three hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Paintings of the Gurus and of Sikh history hang in homes, gurdwara halls and museums; Sikhs differ on how such pictures should be used, and they are not worshiped as the Guru.
